```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE)
```

prolfqua works on one table in long format, one row per feature (protein, peptide or precursor) and sample, together with an `AnalysisConfiguration` that says which column holds what. This vignette builds both from a table you already have.

# Output of quantification software

For the output of common quantification software, the [prolfquapp](https://github.com/prolfqua/prolfquapp) package has readers that return a ready `LFQData` object together with the protein annotation:

- DIA-NN: `prolfquapp::preprocess_DIANN()`
- MaxQuant: `prolfquapp::preprocess_MQ_peptide()`
- Spectronaut: `prolfquapp::preprocess_BGS()`
- FragPipe: `prolfquapp::preprocess_FP_PSM()`
- MSstats-formatted tables: `prolfquapp::preprocess_MSstats()`

They need the FASTA file used for the search. prolfquapp is installed from GitHub; see its README. The rest of this vignette shows how to build an `LFQData` object from any other table.

# A table in wide format

Frequently, the data are available in tables where the rows are proteins and the columns are samples.
In the example, the first column holds the protein identifier and the other columns the intensities of samples A to D.

```{r sampleDataFrame}
df <- data.frame(
  protein_Id = c("tr|A|HUMAN", "tr|B|HUMAN", "tr|C|HUMAN", "tr|D|HUMAN"),
  Intensity_A = c(100, 10000, 10, NA),
  Intensity_B = c(NA, 9000, 20, 100),
  Intensity_C = c(200, 8000, NA, 150),
  Intensity_D = c(130, 11000, 50, 50)
)
df
```

This table can be converted into a table in long format:

```{r pivot2Long}
table_long <- tidyr::pivot_longer(df, dplyr::starts_with("Intensity_"), names_to = "Sample", values_to = "Intensity")
table_long
```

In addition you need a table with the sample annotation. In this example there are three groups, A, B and C.

```{r annotationDataFrame}
annot <- data.frame(
  Sample = c("Intensity_A", "Intensity_B", "Intensity_C", "Intensity_D"),
  Group = c("A", "A", "B", "C")
)
```

Join the annotation to the intensities. Protein-level data should also say from how many peptides each protein intensity was computed in each sample; some methods use this count as a weight. It is unknown here, so it is set to 1.

```{r addAnnotation}
table_long <- dplyr::inner_join(annot, table_long, by = "Sample")
table_long$nr_children <- 1L
```

Create an `AnalysisConfiguration` and name the columns: which one identifies the sample and which one holds the intensities.

```{r createConfig}
config <- prolfqua::AnalysisConfiguration$new()
config$file_name <- "Sample"
config$work_intensity <- "Intensity"
```

The columns identifying the measured features, which are proteins, peptides or precursors, are described using the named list `hierarchy`. The values of the list are the column names, while the names are arbitrary as long as they are valid R column names. Here we use the same names as the column names.

The list `factors` points to the columns with the explanatory variables of the analysis (Group).

```{r addFactors}
config$hierarchy[["protein_Id"]] <- "protein_Id"
config$factors[["Group"]] <- "Group"
```

`setup_analysis()` checks the table against the configuration and completes it, and `LFQData$new()` creates the data object.

```{r buildLFQData}
analysis_data <- prolfqua::setup_analysis(table_long, config)
lfqdata <- prolfqua::LFQData$new(analysis_data, config)
```

```{r basicPlotting}
lfqdata$hierarchy_counts()
smrz <- lfqdata$get_Summariser()
smrz$plot_hierarchy_counts_sample()
```

# A matrix with row and sample annotation

When the intensities are already a matrix, with features in rows and samples in columns, plus a table describing the rows and one describing the samples, `lfqdata_from_wide()` builds the `LFQData` object directly. It is the inverse of `LFQData$data_wide(as.matrix = TRUE)`; row `i` of the matrix belongs to row `i` of the row table.

```{r fromWide}
intensities <- as.matrix(df[, -1])
rowdata <- data.frame(protein_Id = df$protein_Id)
samples <- data.frame(
  sampleName = annot$Sample,
  Sample = annot$Sample,
  Group = annot$Group
)
children <- matrix(1L, nrow = nrow(intensities), ncol = ncol(intensities), dimnames = dimnames(intensities))
from_wide <- prolfqua::lfqdata_from_wide(
  list(Intensity = intensities, nr_children = children),
  rowdata,
  samples,
  config
)
from_wide$hierarchy_counts()
```

# A table in long format

Long tables, such as the reports of Spectronaut, Skyline or DIA-NN, need only a configuration. Here a simulated peptide table stands in for such a report:

```{r readInData}
dataLongFormat <- prolfqua::sim_lfq_data(n_proteins = 20, peptide = TRUE)
head(dataLongFormat)
```

The sample is in the column `sample` and the intensity in `abundance`. Each row is one peptide, so it counts as one child of its protein:

```{r defineAnalysisTable}
dataLongFormat$nr_children <- 1L
config <- prolfqua::AnalysisConfiguration$new()
config$file_name <- "sample"
config$work_intensity <- "abundance"
```

The hierarchy has two levels here, protein and peptide. The names of `factors` are the names used in model formulas, figures and legends; they can differ from the column names, for example `config$factors[["Condition"]] <- "R.Condition"` for a Spectronaut report. A table can hold several factors.

```{r defineHierarchyAndFactors}
config$hierarchy[["proteinID"]] <- "proteinID"
config$hierarchy[["peptideID"]] <- "peptideID"
config$factors[["group"]] <- "group"
```

`setup_analysis()` creates from the long table a table that matches the configuration, and `LFQData$new()` the data object, which is the start of every further analysis.

```{r mateDataAndConfig}
analysis_data <- prolfqua::setup_analysis(dataLongFormat, config)
lfqdata <- prolfqua::LFQData$new(analysis_data, config)
lfqdata$summarize_hierarchy()
```

With this, it is possible for example to use the `get_Summariser` function to visualize and summarise the data.

```{r doBarPlotPerSample, fig.cap="Number of peptides found in each sample", fig.align="center", fig.height=5}
smrz <- lfqdata$get_Summariser()
smrz$plot_hierarchy_counts_sample()
```

The `prolfqua` package is described in [@Wolski2023prolfqua].
